POLS*3230.Description: This course explores the impact of modern science and technology, and its impact on the western tradition of justice from the seventeenth century to the twentieth century. It will explore this theme in writers such as Thomas Hobbes, Jonathan Swift, J-J Rousseau, Edmund Burke, Friedrich Nietzsche and George Grant. The exact selection of thinkers will vary from year to year and students are advised to check the course outline.
POLS*3230.Requisites: POLS*2000 or PHIL*2280   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3250.Title: POLS*3250 Public Policy: Challenges & Pr (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3250.Description: This course covers the dominant theories that explain the origins and character of public policy in Canada, and other countries. The focus will be on both governmental and nongovernmental actors.
POLS*3250.Requisites:
POLS*2230 or POLS*2250
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3300.Title: POLS*3300 Governing Criminal Justice (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3300.Description: The course provides an overview of the policy process and outcomes of the Canadian criminal justice system. Particular emphasis is placed on examining, using various public policy and public management perspectives, the practices and interactions of governmental agencies within the system, such as police agencies and boards, departments of Justice, Solicitor-General, corrections and parole agencies, courts and the legal profession.
POLS*3300.Offering: Also offered  through Distance Education  format.
POLS*3300.Restriction: This is a Priority  Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to  particular programs or specializations or  semester levels during certain periods. Please  see the departmental website for more  information.
POLS*3300.Requisites:
1 of POLS*2350, POLS*2250, POLS*2300
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3320.Title: POLS*3320 Politics of Aid & Development (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3320.Description: This course examines the motivations and mechanisms by which industrialized states have designed and implemented foreign aid programs and policy, primarily since the end of the Second World War. Particular emphasis will be placed on the role of multilateral, bilateral and nongovernmental organizations in the delivery of development assistance and humanitarian relief.
POLS*3320.Requisites: 1 of IDEV*2000, IDEV*2400, POLS*2080   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3340.Title: POLS*3340 Indigenous Politics in Canada (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3340.Description: This course provides an overview of the relationship between the Canadian state and Indigenous peoples by critically analyzing key historical and contemporary legal, political, and social developments in this evolving relationship.
POLS*3340.Offering: Also offered through Distance Education format.
POLS*3340.Requisites: 1 of ANTH*2660, HIST*2090, HIST*2600, INDG*1000, POLS*2230, POLS*2300   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3350.Title: POLS*3350 Comparative Law and Courts (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3350.Description: The course compares legal systems and judicial processes (such as judicial selection, decision-making, and accountability) across jurisdictions and explores similarities and differences in legal and judicial systems. The course critically analyzes the implications of these differences, such as in terms of judicial power, access to justice, and the protection of rights.
POLS*3350.Requisites: 1 of IDEV*2400, POLS*2100, POLS*2350   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3370.Title: POLS*3370 Enviro Politics & Governance (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3370.Description: This course examines environmental politics and governance in Canada as well as in comparative and international contexts. This is accomplished by surveying how various political, legal, administrative, and private-public actors and processes influence the development and implementation of environmental policy.
POLS*3370.Offering: Also offered through Distance  Education format.
POLS*3370.Requisites:
7.50 credits
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3440.Title: POLS*3440 Corrupt. Scandal & Pol. Ethics (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3440.Description: This course will introduce students to the phenomenon of political corruption and the study of its incidence. Attention will be paid to historical examples, contemporary scandals, and analytical articles, dealing with the nature, causes and effects, and proposed cures of political corruption, and the ethical dilemmas inherent in political life.
POLS*3440.Offering: Also  offered through Distance Education  format.
POLS*3440.Requisites:
5.00 credits
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3470.Title: POLS*3470 Bus/Gov't Relations in Canada (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3470.Description: The public and private sectors in Canada have become more and more interrelated in recent years as evidenced by tax and expenditure policies, the role of regulation and public enterprise, and the increasing emphasis on consultation and co-ordination. This course examines the evolving relationship between governments and the private sector in Canada, including business (both large and small), organized labour, specific sectors such as agriculture and consumer affairs and voluntary organizations.
POLS*3470.Requisites: 1 of POLS*1400, POLS*2230, POLS*2250   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3490.Title: POLS*3490 Conflict & Conflict Resolution (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3490.Description: This course will examine the growing body of literature which considers violent conflict and its management. Materials are organized to reflect the trajectory of many contemporary conflicts: from explanations for violence, to identifying conditions and means to resolve conflict and, finally, to post-conflict governance.
POLS*3490.Restriction: This is a Priority  Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to  particular programs or specializations or  semester levels during certain periods. Please  see the departmental website for more  information.
POLS*3490.Requisites:
1 of POLS*1500, POLS*2100, POLS*2200
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3670.Title: POLS*3670 Comparative Public Policy (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3670.Description: This course examines the political factors that shape the policymaking process. Using the major theoretical perspectives, the course compares public policies in different countries. Empirically, the focus is on a variety of pressing issues that societies currently face.
POLS*3670.Requisites:
1 of POLS*2080, POLS*2100, POLS*2230
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3710.Title: POLS*3710 Sex and the Law (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3710.Description: This course introduces students to the politics surrounding the regulation of sex and sexuality. It analyzes how the distribution of power through formal and informal political institutions determines how we understand sex, who is considered a sex agent and what types of sexual behaviour are legally and ethically acceptable. Special attention is given to the relationship between sex, gender and sexual orientation.
POLS*3710.Requisites: 1 of PHIL*2060, POLS*2000, POLS*2150, SOAN*2400   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3790.Title: POLS*3790 Money, Power & Global Politics (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3790.Description: This course examines major features of the contemporary international political economy, treating major theories and concepts within this approach to international relations (hegemony, globalization, interdependence, world systems theory, etc.) and focusing on the operation of key international institutions and regimes (i.e. communications, trade and transport policy).
POLS*3790.Requisites: 1 of GEOG*2230, IDEV*2000, IDEV*2500, POLS*2080, POLS*2100, POLS*2200   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*3850.Title: POLS*3850 Experiential Learning in Polit (0.5 Credits)
POLS*3850.Description: This course allows students to reflect upon their involvement in some form of politically related activity, including simulations, volunteer programs, or internship work with government or non-government organizations. The student must find a faculty member from the Department of Political Science willing to act as a supervisor for the course. See the Political Science website for the learning contract and other requirements that must be completed in advance of registering for this course.
POLS*3850.Requisites: 10.00 credits, 2.00 of which must be in Political Science.   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4050.Title: POLS*4050 Adv Topics in Law & Politics (1 Credits)
POLS*4050.Description: This course explores advanced topics in law and politics depending on the interests of the instructor. Potential topics include investigating the law and politics of social change or analyzing debates about the political power of courts in Canada or in comparative perspectives.
POLS*4050.Restriction: POLS*4060. CJPP and CJPP:C students are restricted to a maximum of 3.00 credits in SOC and POLS 4000-level CJPP restricted electives. This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or specializations or semester levels during certain periods. Please see the departmental website for more information.
POLS*4050.Requisites: 12.50 credits including 1 of POLS*3020, POLS*3130, POLS*3140, POLS*3350   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4060.Title: POLS*4060 Adv Lecture in Law & Politics (0.5 Credits)
POLS*4060.Description: This advanced lecture course explores topics in law and politics. Specific topics vary depending on the interests of the instructor. Potential topics include the relationship between law and social change, human rights, the relationship between law and power, judicial decision-making, and the relationship between law, class, gender, race, and sexuality.
POLS*4060.Restriction: POLS*4050. CJPP and CJPP:C students are restricted to a maximum of 3.00 credits in SOC and POLS 4000-level CJPP restricted electives. This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or specializations or semester levels during certain periods. Please see the departmental website for more information.
POLS*4060.Requisites: 12.50 credits including 1 of POLS*3020, POLS*3130, POLS*3140, POLS*3350   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4070.Title: POLS*4070 Courts & Parliament (1 Credits)
POLS*4070.Description: The course critically examines the complex relationship between the judiciary and representative institutions. By comparing the treatment of current political controversies (assisted suicide, prostitution, drug treatment), students will better appreciate the often-subtle exchanges between the two institutions and further enhance their research abilities in regards to both legal and legislative processes.
POLS*4070.Restriction: This is a Priority Access Course. CJPP and CJPP:C students are restricted to a maximum of 3.00 credits in SOC and POLS 4000-level CJPP restricted electives. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or specializations or semester levels during certain periods. Please see the departmental website for more information.
POLS*4070.Requisites: 12.50 credits including 1 of POLS*2350, POLS*3130, POLS*3300   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4250.Title: POLS*4250 Topics in Public Management (1 Credits)
POLS*4250.Description: This course will examine various topics related to governance, such as public management reform, public sector leadership, third sector organizations or budgeting and human resources.
POLS*4250.Restriction: POLS*4270. CJPP and CJPP:C students are restricted to a maximum of 3.00 credits in SOC and POLS 4000-level CJPP restricted electives. This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or specializations or semester levels during certain periods. Please see the departmental website for more information.
POLS*4250.Requisites: 12.50 credits including (POLS*2250, 1.00 credits at the 3000 level in the Public Policy, Governance and Law stream or the Canadian Politics stream). Streams are defined under the Political Science Major.   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4290.Title: POLS*4290 Why Public Policy Matters (1 Credits)
POLS*4290.Description: This course critically explores the ethical dimensions of public policy, analyzing how governments address issues of general concern through provision, prohibition, or both. Emphasizing the high stakes nature of policy making, the course examines principles and values through the framework of applied ethics, using ethical theories to assess practical matters. Students engage with ethical theories that enable critical evaluation of contested policy issues.
POLS*4290.Requisites: 12.50 credits and 0.50 credits in the Public Policy, Governance and Law stream or the Political Thought stream at the third-year level. Streams are defined under the Political Science major.   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4790.Title: POLS*4790 Lecture Courts and Parliament (0.5 Credits)
POLS*4790.Description: The course analyzes the relationship between courts and the elected branches of government in Canada and a comparative perspective. Using relevant examples, the course examines how courts and legislatures participate in constitutional interpretation and explores debates about the appropriate role of courts and legislatures in political life.
POLS*4790.Restriction: POLS*4070. CJPP and CJPP:C students are restricted to a maximum of 3.00 credits in SOC and POLS 4000-level CJPP restricted electives. This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or specializations or semester levels during certain periods. Please see the departmental website for more information.
POLS*4790.Requisites: 12.50 credits and 0.50 credit at the third-year level from the Public Policy, Governance and Law stream (see streams in the POLS major).   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4900.Title: POLS*4900 Seminar in Political Science (1 Credits)
POLS*4900.Description: This seminar-based course explores a current issue in Political Science. Topics will vary from year to year and will reflect the research and teaching interests of the faculty member directing the course. Information on the topic of the current offering can be found on the departmental website.
POLS*4900.Requisites:
14.00 credits, including 1.00 credits in Political Science  at the 3000 level.
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4910.Title: POLS*4910 Sel Topics in Political Sci (0.5 Credits)
POLS*4910.Description: This course provides for independent reading and research in selected areas of the discipline not covered by regular course offerings. Prior to enrollment in the course, approval must be obtained from a member of the department willing to supervise the research. Students should approach potential supervisors with a proposal for readings and research, which may include reflection and expansion on a subject matter addressed in previous course assignments.
POLS*4910.Requisites:
1.50 credits at the 3000 level in Political Science or  equivalent
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4930.Title: POLS*4930 Selected Topics in Poli Sci (1 Credits)
POLS*4930.Description: This course provides for independent reading and research in selected areas of the discipline not covered by regular course offerings. Prior to enrollment in the course, approval must be obtained from a member of the department willing to supervise the research. Students should approach potential supervisors with a proposal for readings and research, which may include reflection and expansion on a subject matter addressed in previous course assignments.
POLS*4930.Requisites:
1.50 credits at the 3000 level in Political Science or  equivalent
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4970.Title: POLS*4970 Hons. Poli. Sci. Research I (0.5 Credits)
POLS*4970.Description: This is Part I of the Honours Essay. Students complete the necessary reading and research for their Honours Essay under the supervision of a department advisor. A research proposal is expected by the end of the semester. Political science majors who wish to pursue an honours thesis must register in this course in their 7th semester. Student selection of an approved subject area and instructor must be completed in the semester previous to enrolment in this course.
POLS*4970.Restriction: Instructor consent required. CJPP and CJPP:C students are restricted to a maximum of 3.00 credits in SOC and POLS 4000-level CJPP restricted electives.
POLS*4970.Requisites:
70% average in all POLS courses. Recommendation: Students  with less than a 75% average are advised not to take this  course.
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POLS*4980.Title: POLS*4980 Hons. Poli. Sci. Research II (0.5 Credits)
POLS*4980.Description: This is Part II of the Honours Essay. Students organize and write their essays under the supervision of their advisor. Major honours political science students must register in this course in their 8th semester.
POLS*4980.Restriction: Instructor consent required. CJPP and CJPP:C students are restricted to a maximum of 3.00 credits in SOC and POLS 4000-level CJPP restricted electives.
POLS*4980.Requisites:
POLS*4970
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POPM*3240.Title: POPM*3240 Epidemiology (0.5 Credits)
POPM*3240.Description: The course examines the basic concepts of health and disease in populations. Methods used in descriptive and analytic epidemiological studies, including the design, analysis and interpretation of results for observational studies and field trials are presented.
POPM*3240.Offering: Also offered  through Distance Education  format.
POPM*3240.Requisites: (BIOL*1080 or BIOL*1090), (1 of SOAN*2120, STAT*2040, STAT*2230)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POPM*4040.Title: POPM*4040 Epidem of Food-borne Diseases (0.5 Credits)
POPM*4040.Description: This course examines the epidemiology and prevention of food-borne infections and intoxications, including those of both microbiological and chemical origin. Drawing on outbreak investigations, surveys, risk assessments, government surveillance systems and basic research, the biological, ecological, socio-economic and public health context of these diseases will be discussed.
POPM*4040.Requisites:
1 of FOOD*3230, POPM*3240
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

POPM*4230.Title: POPM*4230 Animal Health (0.5 Credits)
POPM*4230.Description: This course examines the causes and effects of important diseases of food animals in Canada, with a focus on dairy cattle. Elements of physiology, epidemiology, microbiology, nutrition, and production management are integrated into a health management approach emphasizing disease prevention. The course is directed at senior undergraduate students with interest in and knowledge of, food animal production agriculture.
POPM*4230.Restriction: This is a Priority Access  Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular  programs or specializations or semester levels  during certain periods. See the departmental  website for more information.
POPM*4230.Requisites: 1 of ANSC*2340, ANSC*3080, (ONEH*2000, POPM*3240)     - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*1000.Title: PSYC*1000 Introduction to Psychology (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*1000.Description: This is an introduction to the content and methods of psychology. It will cover the major areas such as neuroscience, sensation and perception, learning, cognition, motivation, human development, personality, psychopathology and its treatment, and social psychology.
PSYC*1000.Offering: Also offered through Distance  Education format.
PSYC*1000.Restriction: This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.

PSYC*1010.Title: PSYC*1010 Making Sense of Data (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*1010.Description: This course introduces research designs and quantitative approaches used in psychological science, with an emphasis on conceptual understanding. Specific topics include distributions, meta-analysis, confidence intervals and p-values, effect size, and regression, as well as the differences between descriptive, correlational, and experimental research designs.
PSYC*1010.Restriction: STAT*2040, STAT*2060, STAT*2080, STAT*2120, STAT*2230. This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*1010.Requisites:
PSYC*1000
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*2020.Title: PSYC*2020 Clinical Psyc & Mental Health (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*2020.Description: This course is an introduction to clinical psychology and mental health including a multidimensional conceptualization of mental health, assessment, diagnosis, and treatment. Common psychological disorders will be explored with respect to etiology, assessment, current diagnosis and classification, as well as treatment. Emphasis will be given to broad empirical research and to the experiences of individuals with these disorders.
PSYC*2020.Offering: Also offered through Distance Education format.
PSYC*2020.Restriction: This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*2020.Requisites:
PSYC*1000
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*2070.Title: PSYC*2070 Teams Leadership & Prof Beh (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*2070.Description: The course will focus on the theory and practical application of Organizational Psychology with regard to leadership, teams, and professional behaviour. The course will provide students with opportunities to assess their leadership and teamwork skills, as well as active learning activities to practice these skills. Key topics will include work motivation, time management, personal organizational skills, goal setting, conflict management, social influence and stress management.
PSYC*2070.Requisites: 4.00 credits including PSYC*1000   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*2310.Title: PSYC*2310 Social Psychology (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*2310.Description: This course introduces students to the field of social psychology. Major topics introduced will include: social influence, social cognition, attitude, stereotype and prejudice, the self, attraction and interpersonal relationships, group processes and intergroup relations. The course also aims for students to use the knowledge acquired to think critically about how their actions and those of others are influenced by social forces. In addition, the course aims to introduce students to the role of culture in shaping thoughts and behaviour and to provide them an opportunity to appreciate diverse perspectives.
PSYC*2310.Offering: Also offered through  Distance Education format.
PSYC*2310.Restriction: This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*2310.Requisites: PSYC*1000   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*2330.Title: PSYC*2330 Principles of Learning (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*2330.Description: This course provides a detailed description of principles and concepts of learning and motivation, as well as an introduction to their underlying neurobiological mechanisms. Through the examination of empirical evidence in the fields of Psychology and Behavioural Neuroscience, this course offers a comprehensive description of the role of conditioning in normal and abnormal behaviours.
PSYC*2330.Offering: Also offered through Distance Education format.
PSYC*2330.Restriction: This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*2330.Requisites:
PSYC*1000
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*2360.Title: PSYC*2360 Psych Methods & Statistics (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*2360.Description: This course builds on students' understanding of basic psychological research methods and statistics, with an emphasis on designing, interpreting, and communicating research. Topics covered throughout the term may include: research ethics, the scientific method, qualitative and quantitative measures, reliability and validity, complex research designs using multiple predictor or independent variables, and the reading and writing of psychological journal articles.
PSYC*2360.Requisites: PSYC*1000, (1 of PSYC*1010, STAT*2040, STAT*2060, STAT*2080, STAT*2120, STAT*2230)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*2410.Title: PSYC*2410 Behavioural Neuroscience I (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*2410.Description: This course is a general introduction to the structure and function of the nervous system. The physiological basis of sensory (input) systems and the motor (output) system are examined as are central physiological bases of processes such as learning and memory.
PSYC*2410.Offering: Also offered  through Distance Education format.
PSYC*2410.Restriction: NEUR*2000. Not available to students registered in the BSCH.NEUR and BSCH.NEUR:C. This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*2410.Requisites: PSYC*1000   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*2450.Title: PSYC*2450 Developmental Psychology (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*2450.Description: This course is an introduction to and an analysis of the major theories of developmental psychology. Emphasis will be placed on the processes of development in the child including physical growth, perception, cognition, personality and interactions with the social environment. The application of developmental psychology to educational and social issues will be discussed.
PSYC*2450.Offering: Also offered through  Distance Education format.
PSYC*2450.Restriction: FRHD*2270. This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*2450.Requisites: PSYC*1000   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*2650.Title: PSYC*2650 Cognitive Psychology (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*2650.Description: This course is an introduction to cognitive processes, including topics in the areas of attention, memory, language and reasoning. Students will be exposed to and participate in on-line laboratory demonstrations and experiments.
PSYC*2650.Offering: Also offered through  Distance Education format.
PSYC*2650.Restriction: This  is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*2650.Requisites: PSYC*1000   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3000.Title: PSYC*3000 Historical & Crit Persp on Psy (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3000.Description: The purpose of this course is to help students understand the socio-historical and theoretical context of modern psychological research and practice. This includes: 1) evaluating basic assumptions underlying modern psychology by drawing on historical, theoretical and philosophical perspectives, and 2) investigating historical and current controversies within psychology. Topics may include the question of psychology's scientific status, the assumptions embedded in psychological theory and research methodology, social constructionism, free will/agency, and the relations between psychology, power, ethics, and politics.
PSYC*3000.Requisites: PSYC*2070, PSYC*2360, (3 of PSYC*2020, PSYC*2310, PSYC*2330, PSYC*2390, PSYC*2410, PSYC*2450, PSYC*2650, PSYC*2740)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3020.Title: PSYC*3020 Psychology of Law (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3020.Description: An examination of psychological methods, findings and theories in the study of law. Topics will include the fallibility of the eyewitness; juror decisional processes; credibility of witnesses and attorneys; socialization into legal systems, police behaviour, etc.
PSYC*3020.Offering: Also offered  through Distance Education  format.
PSYC*3020.Requisites:
2.50 credits in Psychology or PSYC*2310
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3240.Title: PSYC*3240 Independent Research (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3240.Description: This course provides individual students with hands-on experience conducting a research project. Students are supervised directly by a faculty member as they conduct an in-depth investigation of a specific topic within psychology. Typically, the course involves both the practice and reporting of research. Through this experience students will develop a broader appreciation of the relations between knowledge, theory and research while acquiring basic skills in research methodologies and modes of inquiry. In addition, students will develop their written and oral communication skills (e.g., integration of relevant literature, reporting of research). Course registration requires the signature of the Psychology Academic Manager. This signature is contingent upon the student demonstrating they have obtained a faculty supervisor's signature and satisfy the course prerequisites. Please see the Psychology department website for more information. https://www.uoguelph.ca/psychology/
PSYC*3240.Requisites:
2.50 credits in Psychology including PSYC*2360
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3270.Title: PSYC*3270 Cognitive Neuroscience (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3270.Description: This course provides an overview of the neural process that support cognitive abilities such as attention, perception, memory, emotion, and reasoning. An emphasis is placed on primary research with the goal of revealing the types of methods that cognitive neuroscientists use, and types of questions that they ask, as they try to understand the relationship between our minds and brains.
PSYC*3270.Restriction: This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*3270.Requisites:
1 of NEUR*2000, PSYC*2390, PSYC*2410, PSYC*2650
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3290.Title: PSYC*3290 Statistical Analysis in Psych (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3290.Description: This course focuses on training students in the quantitative analysis and communications skills needed to become a researcher in psychology. Students conduct a correlation-based meta-analysis to help them concretely understand sampling distributions and the difficulties associated with obtaining study results that replicate. This meta-analytic foundation is then leveraged to teach traditional psychological analysis techniques (e.g., t-test, analysis of variance, and bi-variate/multiple regression) with an emphasis on maximizing factors that increase the probability of study findings that replicate. The value of interpreting results using effect sizes with confidence intervals is discussed and the logic of null-hypothesis testing is briefly reviewed.
PSYC*3290.Requisites:
2.50 credits in Psychology including PSYC*2360
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3330.Title: PSYC*3330 Memory and Attention (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3330.Description: This course provides an overview of attention and memory: how we prioritize some objects and events over others and how such prior experience influences our subsequent thoughts, feelings and actions. The course will cover what is known about memory and attention from research in the overlapping fields of cognitive psychology, neuropsychology, and cognitive neuroscience.
PSYC*3330.Requisites: 2.50 credits in Psychology including (PSYC*2650 or PSYC*3270)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3350.Title: PSYC*3350 Cross-Cultural Psychology (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3350.Description: This course provides an examination of cultural differences from the perspective of psychology, and of individual and group relations within and between culturally diverse societies. The primary goal of this course is to provide a framework and knowledge base with which to understand the various contexts, processes and outcomes of intercultural contact.
PSYC*3350.Requisites:
2.50 credits in Psychology including PSYC*2310
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3470.Title: PSYC*3470 Putting Psychology to Work (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3470.Description: This course provides students with the opportunity to prepare for the transition to post-graduate programs and work, by exploring psychology as it relates to work. Topics include: the history of work and industrial psychology, career management, job analysis, recruitment, selection, employment law, compensation and benefits, performance appraisal, training and development, as well as succession planning.
PSYC*3470.Offering: Also offered through Distance Education format.
PSYC*3470.Restriction: Restricted to BAH.PSYC, BAH.PSYC:C, and BAG.PSYC. This is a Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.
PSYC*3470.Requisites:
PSYC*2070, PSYC*2360, (2 of PSYC*2020, PSYC*2310,  PSYC*2450, PSYC*2740), (1 of PSYC*2330, PSYC*2390,  PSYC*2410, PSYC*2650)
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3490.Title: PSYC*3490 Social & Organizational Psych (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3490.Description: A number of applied issues will be examined from a social and organizational psychological perspective. The topics will include health and well-being; attributions and person perception; intergroup relations and prejudice; and social influence. Students will learn how to apply psychological theories and research to understand and ameliorate applied issues.
PSYC*3490.Requisites:
3.00 credits in Psychology including PSYC*2070, PSYC*2310
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3800.Title: PSYC*3800 Psychology and Education (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3800.Description: The application of psychological principles and techniques to the study of the educational process.
PSYC*3800.Requisites: FRHD*2270 or PSYC*1000   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*3910.Title: PSYC*3910 Psychology Externship (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*3910.Description: An independent program of study formally integrating the student's academic study with one or more work experiences, to be decided by the student in consultation with the supervisory faculty prior to registration in the course. In order to qualify for this course, the student must be employed in a work setting at the time of registration to help ensure that a suitable project is feasible in the context of a work placement or employment. The department is not responsible for obtaining employment. The course project is aimed at making a significant contribution to the work setting. The student must consult with the supervisory faculty before selecting or registering for the course. (Enrolment is limited. Not open to co-op students.)
PSYC*3910.Requisites:
PSYC*2070, PSYC*2360, (2 of PSYC*2020, PSYC*2310,  PSYC*2450, PSYC*2740), (1 of PSYC*2330, PSYC*2390,  PSYC*2410, PSYC*2650)
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4240.Title: PSYC*4240 Adv Independent Research (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*4240.Description: This course provides individual students with hands-on experience conducting a research project. Students are supervised directly by a faculty member as they conduct an in-depth investigation of a specific topic within psychology. Typically, the course involves both the practice and reporting of research. Students will apply the research and communication skills they have acquired through prior coursework in order to work more independently. Course registration requires the signature of the Psychology Academic Manager. This signature is contingent upon the student demonstrating they have obtained a faculty supervisor's signature and satisfy the course prerequisites. Please see the Psychology department website for more information. https://www.uoguelph.ca/psychology/
PSYC*4240.Requisites: 14.00 credits including (PSYC*3290, 1.00 credits in Psychology at the 3000 level)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4290.Title: PSYC*4290 Psychological Measurement (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*4290.Description: This course focuses on training students how to conduct research such that measurement theory guides measure selection and construction. Consequences of measurement theory (reliability/validity) for the accuracy of research findings and interpretation of test scores are also covered. A variety of individual difference variables are examined with an emphasis on how measurement strategies differ depending on the nature of the
PSYC*4290.Requisites: PSYC*3290   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4330.Title: PSYC*4330 Adv Topics in I/O Psychology (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*4330.Description: Students will examine theoretical and methodological issues in selected topic areas of industrial/organizational psychology. Selected topic areas may include diversity issues, trust and justice, job performance, employment selection, and stress and well-being. Specific topics, to be announced prior to course selection, will vary according to the interests of the instructor of the course.
PSYC*4330.Requisites: 14.00 credits including PSYC*3290, (1 of PSYC*2070, PSYC*3490)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4460.Title: PSYC*4460 Adv Top in Clin & App Dvt Psyc (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*4460.Description: This course covers issues and theories in clinical or applied developmental psychology. Topics may include pediatric (child health) psychology, attachment relationships, non-suicidal self-injury, and aggression. The selected topic, to be announced prior to course selection, will vary on the basis of the expertise of the instructor.
PSYC*4460.Requisites: 14.00 credits including PSYC*2020, PSYC*3290, (1 of FRHD*2270, PSYC*2450, PSYC*2740)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4470.Title: PSYC*4470 Adv Topics in Beh & Cogn Neur (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*4470.Description: Major areas of contemporary behavioural or cognitive neuroscience will be covered in a seminar format. Selected topic areas may include the neural basis of learning, memory, attention, sensation, and perception. The selected topic, to be announced prior to course selection, will vary on the basis of the expertise of the instructor.
PSYC*4470.Requisites:
PSYC*3270, (NEUR*2000 or PSYC*2410)
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4540.Title: PSYC*4540 Practical Applications of Psyc (1 Credits)
PSYC*4540.Description: This is a required capstone course for students in Psychology's BA and BSC Honours major programs, excepting those who are taking the Honours Thesis courses (PSYC*4780, 4880). The course adopts a problem-based learning approach in which students will be presented with problems resembling those that they will face in their professional and personal lives. Students will apply their psychological knowledge and skills to analyze the problem, consider solutions, and communicate recommendations to hypothetical stakeholders.
PSYC*4540.Requisites: 14.00 credits including PSYC*3290, (PSYC*3000 or 7.50 credits in Psychology)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4780.Title: PSYC*4780 Advanced Quantitative Methods (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*4780.Description: As a companion to honours thesis, this course focuses on advanced quantitative research methods and statistical techniques, cumulating in the creation of statistical research plans for student theses in a manner consistent with contemporary standards. A key feature of the course is learning research designs and workflows that are consistent with disciplinary standards and likely to create replicable study results. Students will focus on the correspondence between complex designs and the statistical techniques that can be used to analyze the data resulting from such designs. In addition to readings, lectures, and in-class exercises, students will be guided through the process of creating scripts for analyzing quantitative data and reporting on an empirical investigation.
PSYC*4780.Requisites: 14.00 credits including (1 of PSYC*3290, STAT*2050, STAT*2090)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4790.Title: PSYC*4790 Qualitative Methods (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*4790.Description: This course examines qualitative methods in psychology. Students will be exposed to key theoretical and methodological foundations for conducting qualitative research. Students will also be guided through conducting qualitative data analysis.
PSYC*4790.Requisites: 14.00 credits   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4870.Title: PSYC*4870 Honours Thesis I (0.5 Credits)
PSYC*4870.Description: Under individual faculty supervision, students plan, develop, and write a research proposal and prepare an extensive review paper on their area of research. Group sessions are held on research ethics, subject protocols and computer data handling techniques. This course will be graded on a Pass/Fail basis. Note that enrolment in this course is limited and academic records are used for student selection. Course registration requires the signature of the Course Instructor. This signature is contingent upon the student demonstrating they have obtained a Thesis Supervisor's signature on the department's Thesis Registration Form and have an academic standing appropriate for application to graduate programs (see Graduate Advisory under

14.00 credits including (1 of NEUR*3500, PSYC*3000, 7.50  credits in Psychology)
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

PSYC*4880.Title: PSYC*4880 Honours Thesis II (1 Credits)
PSYC*4880.Description: This course is a continuation of PSYC*4870. Students conduct research and write an undergraduate thesis under the direction of a faculty member.
PSYC*4880.Requisites:
PSYC*4870
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

REAL*1820.Title: REAL*1820 Introduction to Real Estate (0.5 Credits)
REAL*1820.Description: This survey course acquaints students with the theories, practices and principles of real estate and housing. Topics include how real estate assets and markets differ from other assets: including real estate economics, financing, development, appraisal, brokerage, zoning, property management, taxation, and government involvement. Many property types may be considered, including residential, multi-residential, office, industrial, and retail.
REAL*1820.Department: Department of Marketing and Consumer Studies

REAL*2850.Title: REAL*2850 Service Learning in Housing (0.5 Credits)
REAL*2850.Description: This course provides an introduction to ethics and social capital as they apply to the housing and real estate industries. Students will be required to participate in a 10-15 hour service learning exercise where they volunteer for a frontline housing agency/provider. They will then share their experiences with their classmates during the final week of classes.
REAL*2850.Department: Department of Marketing and Consumer Studies
REAL*2850.Requisites:
4.00 credits
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

REAL*3810.Title: REAL*3810 Real Estate Market Analysis (0.5 Credits)
REAL*3810.Description: In this course students examine supply and demand for real estate now and in the future in order to make better decisions. The course focuses on using various research methodologies to define the scope of analysis; identify data needs; collect information from various sources, evaluate their reliability and interpret the results. Applications to different property types are discussed. Current market trends are also examined.
REAL*3810.Department: Department of Marketing and Consumer Studies
REAL*3810.Requisites:
REAL*1820, (ECON*2740 or STAT*2060)
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

REAL*3880.Title: REAL*3880 Topics in Real Estate (0.5 Credits)
REAL*3880.Description: Lecture-discussion or seminar on a selected topic related to real estate to be conducted by faculty with special interests or expertise in the area. Students should confirm with the department prior to course selection what topic(s), if any, will be offered during specific semesters.
REAL*3880.Department: Department of Marketing and Consumer Studies

REAL*4820.Title: REAL*4820 Real Estate Appraisal (0.5 Credits)
REAL*4820.Description: This course deals with the basic principles involved in valuing real estate. The market comparison, cost and income approaches of appraisal are covered. The major emphasis in the course is on using discounted cash flow projections to value income-producing real estate. The term project involves the use of a spreadsheet program to estimate property value for a property chosen by the student. While valuation of single family homes is covered, the main emphasis is on investment real estate.
REAL*4820.Department: Department of Marketing and Consumer Studies
REAL*4820.Requisites:
(1 of CIS*1200, CIS*1500, MCS*2020), (1 of ACCT*2230,  ECON*2560, FIN*2000, REAL*2820)
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

REAL*4840.Title: REAL*4840 Housing & Real Estate Law (0.5 Credits)
REAL*4840.Description: This course lays out the legal principles which guide the expanding and changing body of law dealing with housing and real estate development and forms of occupancy; statutory and regulatory matters are explored.
REAL*4840.Department: Department of Marketing and Consumer Studies
REAL*4840.Requisites:
9.00 credits including REAL*1820, REAL*2820
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

REAL*4870.Title: REAL*4870 Sustainable Real Estate (0.5 Credits)
REAL*4870.Description: This course is designed to give students an understanding of how topics in sustainability and climate change affect and are affected by real estate and urban economics. Students will develop an understanding of the reasons for and benefits of sustainability practices in real estate and planning.
REAL*4870.Department: Department of Marketing and Consumer Studies
REAL*4870.Requisites:
14.00 credits
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*1050.Title: SART*1050 Foundation Studio (0.5 Credits)
SART*1050.Description: This course provides a foundation in the technical and theoretical aspects of contemporary two-dimensional media. Through a combination of lectures, studio projects, readings and a field trip the students will explore perceptual, conceptual and topical dimensions of art making practices.
SART*1050.Restriction: Registration in  semesters one, two, three or four. May not  register in SART*1060 in the same term. This is a  Priority Access Course. Enrolment may be  restricted to particular programs or  specializations during certain periods. Please  see the departmental website for more  information.
SART*1050.Department: School of Fine Art and Music

SART*1060.Title: SART*1060 Core Studio (0.5 Credits)
SART*1060.Description: This course provides a foundation in the technical and theoretical aspects of contemporary three-dimensional and time-based media. Through a combination of lectures, research assignments and studio projects, students will explore perceptual, conceptual and topical dimensions of contemporary art making
SART*1060.Restriction: Registration in semesters one, two, three or four. May not register in SART*1050 in the same term. This is a Priority Access Course. SART*1060.Department: School of Fine Art and Music

SART*1090.Title: SART*1090 Making Comics (0.5 Credits)
SART*1090.Description: This course provides students with the fundamental skills required to generate comics, along with a foundational understanding of comics as both a language and an art form. Through a combination of lectures, demonstrations and short assignments, students will explore comics as a unique semiotic system and expressive medium, culminating in the production of their own autobiographical work.
SART*1090.Department: School of Fine Art and Music

SART*2090.Title: SART*2090 Drawing I (0.5 Credits)
SART*2090.Description: This course will consider the activity of drawing as an ability to work with a varied range of applications - all of them concerned with the investigation and development of idea through making an image. This course is an introduction to the basic concepts, techniques and media of drawing, through disciplined observational and imaginative study.
SART*2090.Restriction: This course is restricted to Studio Art majors or minors who have completed 10.00 credits or less. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*2090.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*2090.Requisites: SART*1050, SART*1060, (1 of ARTH*1220, ARTH*1510, ARTH*1520)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*2200.Title: SART*2200 Painting I (0.5 Credits)
SART*2200.Description: This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamentals of observational painting in oil and acrylic paint. In addition to developing skill in colour-mixing, composition, and using value to create space and form, students will learn proper care for tools and how to prepare supports. Regular discussions of contemporary and relevant historical examples will assist students to understand their work as part of the broader conversation and discourse in painting. Prior or concurrent Drawing classes are recommended.
SART*2200.Restriction: This course is restricted to Studio Art majors or minors who have completed 10.00 credits or less. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*2200.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*2200.Requisites: SART*1050, SART*1060, (1 of ARTH*1220, ARTH*1510, ARTH*1520)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*2300.Title: SART*2300 Sculpture I (0.5 Credits)
SART*2300.Description: This course is an introduction to contemporary sculptural concerns through projects, readings and visual research. Sculptural principles of form and space will be addressed through hands-on engagement with a variety of materials and methods. Readings provide an overview of Modernist sculpture and basic critical theory.
SART*2300.Restriction: This course is restricted to Studio Art majors or minors who have completed 10.00 credits or less. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*2300.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*2300.Requisites: SART*1050, SART*1060, (1 of ARTH*1220, ARTH*1510, ARTH*1520, ARTH*2220)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*2460.Title: SART*2460 Printmaking I (0.5 Credits)
SART*2460.Description: This course is an introduction to the printmaking media of intaglio, relief and silkscreen. Conceptual issues will be examined in relation to the creation of prints with discussions around the characteristics of the edition, the monoprint and the series through printmaking objects and readings.
SART*2460.Restriction: This course is restricted to Studio Art majors or minors who have completed 10.00 credits or less. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*2460.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*2460.Requisites: SART*1050, SART*1060, (1 of ARTH*1220, ARTH*1510, ARTH*1520)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*2610.Title: SART*2610 Photography I (0.5 Credits)
SART*2610.Description: This course is an introduction to the historic, conceptual, and material nature of photography in contemporary art. Course content will include basic digital, analogue and studio techniques, and an exploration of historic techniques such as the Photogram and Camera Obscura. Readings, discussions, and assignments will forge connections between historic and contemporary modes of image making, and will encourage students to experiment with innovative ways of utilizing the photographic medium.
SART*2610.Restriction: This course is restricted to Studio Art majors or minors who have completed 10.00 credits or less. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*2610.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*2610.Requisites: SART*1050, SART*1060, (1 of ARTH*1220, ARTH*1510, ARTH*1520)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*2700.Title: SART*2700 The Digital Image (0.5 Credits)
SART*2700.Description: This course introduces students to current digital image generating technologies. Students will learn common methods for creating digital images using free online tools and open-source desktop and mobile applications. Group projects provide opportunities to research and experiment with various digital tools in a spirit of collaboration and community while strengthening a deeper understanding of the technology within a historical and cultural context. A final individual assignment on the composite will give students the opportunity to explore a combination of digital tools and processes in a creative work grounded in the art historical techniques of montage and collage.
SART*2700.Restriction: Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*2700.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*2700.Requisites: SART*1050, SART*1060, (1 of ARTH*1220, ARTH*1510, ARTH*1520, ARTH*2220)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*2800.Title: SART*2800 Experimental Studio I (0.5 Credits)
SART*2800.Description: This course introduces students to different processes used by the contemporary studio artist, with an emphasis on time-based and interdisciplinary forms of production. Students will be actively engaged in exploring a variety of skills, processes and concepts, in the development of video and audio art, artist multiples, and site-specific interventions. An understanding of the technical, theoretical, and historical concerns of experimental art practices will provide a solid base for upper level courses, where students will develop a stronger capacity to work with media that are appropriate to realize their ideas.
SART*2800.Restriction: This course is restricted to Studio Art majors or minors who have completed 10.00 credits or less. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*2800.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*2800.Requisites: SART*1050, SART*1060, (1 of ARTH*1220, ARTH*1510, ARTH*1520, ARTH*2220)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3090.Title: SART*3090 Drawing II (0.5 Credits)
SART*3090.Description: This course attempts to foster understanding of the basis and technical issues necessary to the making of drawings while introducing the philosophical and critical issues related to the discipline. This course will consider drawing as an activity with a wide range of applications.
SART*3090.Restriction: Registration is limited to  students registered in the Art History or Studio  Art specializations with an average of 70% in all  ARTH and SART course attempts. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*3090.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*3090.Requisites:
SART*2090
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3200.Title: SART*3200 Painting II (0.5 Credits)
SART*3200.Description: In this course, technical, aesthetic and philosophical issues central to contemporary painting will be investigated. These include diverse approaches to representational painting today as well as an introduction to abstraction and other non-representational strategies. Activities such as class discussions, field trips and presentations on contemporary artists will assist students to situate their own developing practices within the field.
SART*3200.Restriction: Registration is limited to students registered in  the Art History or Studio Art specializations  with an average of 70% in all ARTH and SART  course attempts. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*3200.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*3200.Requisites:
SART*2200
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3300.Title: SART*3300 Sculpture II (0.5 Credits)
SART*3300.Description: This is a technical and experimental course in which critical issues in post-modernist and contemporary sculpture will be explored and deployed. Projects will focus on skills training in the wood shop, metal shop and technologies for digital fabrication. Readings will provide an overview of post-modernist and contemporary sculpture.
SART*3300.Restriction: Registration is  limited to students registered in the Art History  or Studio Art specializations with an average of  70% in all ARTH and SART course attempts. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*3300.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*3300.Requisites:
SART*2300
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3600.Title: SART*3600 Digital & Non-Silver Photo (0.5 Credits)
SART*3600.Description: This course combines analogue and digital photographic technologies to connect with the medium's history and materiality. Course content will include medium or large format film photography, darkroom techniques, and an exploration of scale in digital production. Discussions, readings, and seminars will provide students with a critical and historical understanding of the art-making process.
SART*3600.Restriction: Registration is limited to students registered in the Art History or Studio Art specializations with an average of 70% in all ARTH and SART course attempts. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*3600.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*3600.Requisites: SART*2460 or SART*2610   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3660.Title: SART*3660 Printmaking II (0.5 Credits)
SART*3660.Description: This course provides an introduction to stone lithography and will continue to investigate the formal and technical aspects of printmaking techniques covered in SART*2460. Students will be actively engaged in exploring contemporary concerns in printmaking through ideas of dissemination, sequence and systems through scrutiny of printmaking objects and readings.
SART*3660.Restriction: Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*3660.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*3660.Requisites:
SART*2460
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3770.Title: SART*3770 Experimental Studio II (0.5 Credits)
SART*3770.Description: Students will explore and consider the found object and appropriation in art, the use of language and text in art, and other conceptual art practices in various media. In a context of critical reading, writing, class exercises and discussion - students will continue developing their technical skills in video and sound production. We may also consider such forms as collage, the artist book and/or artist multiple, performance, social practice art, and other experimental studio strategies.
SART*3770.Restriction: Registration is limited to students registered in the Art History; Sexualities, Genders, and Social Change; or Studio Art specializations with an average of 70% in all ARTH and SART course attempts. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.
SART*3770.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*3770.Requisites:
SART*2800
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3800.Title: SART*3800 Experiential Learning I (0.5 Credits)
SART*3800.Description: This is an independent study course based on Studio Art-related practical experience. Evaluation will be based on assignments related to work duties. Written proposals, signed by the supervisor and a faculty member, must be submitted to the Director for the School for approval by the last day of course selection in the Fall (for Winter) or Winter (for the following Summer or Fall).
SART*3800.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*3800.Requisites:
3.00 credits in Studio Art
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3900.Title: SART*3900 Experiential Learning II (0.5 Credits)
SART*3900.Description: This course provides students with an opportunity to continue the workplace or activity begun in SART*3800 in greater depth, or to experience a new work/study situation. Evaluation will be based on assignments related to work duties. Written proposals, signed by the supervisor and a faculty member, must be submitted to the Director for the School for approval by the last day of course selection in the Fall (for Winter) or Winter (for the following Summer or Fall) semester.
SART*3900.Department: School of Fine Art and Music
SART*3900.Requisites:
SART*3800 and 3.50 credits in Studio Art
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SART*3950.Title: SART*3950 Exhibitions: Theory & Practice (0.5 Credits)
SART*3950.Description: This course situates exhibition-making as a form of knowledge creation, cultural dialogue, and, in the contemporary context, a collaborative practice between artists, curators, and institutions. With a focus on methodologies, concepts, and strategies that inform exhibition practices, students will explore diverse global examples, ultimately developing their own exhibition proposals. Offered at the Art Gallery of Guelph, the course provides students with hands-on, real-world experience while deepening their understanding of the discursive, theoretical, and political dimensions of exhibitions.
SART*3950.Restriction: Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.

SART*4090.Description: This course will study the technical development of observational drawing as well as the experimental and intentional development of drawing as a contemporary art form. Drawings will be made and discussed with attention to semiotic theory in order to examine the production and interpretation of meaning.
SART*4090.Restriction: Registration is limited to students registered in the Studio Art Major with an average of 70% in all ARTH and SART course attempts. This is a Priority Access Course. SART*4200.Title: SART*4200 Painting III (0.5 Credits)
SART*4200.Description: This course focuses on experimentation as a means to investigate the possibilities available to a contemporary painter. Representational and non-representational approaches will continue to be explored, with emphasis on the development of the student's own research interests. Critical readings, in-class discussions and gallery visits help position their research within the discourse. Paintings will be analyzed with attention to semiotic theory in order to examine the production and interpretation of meaning.
SART*4200.Restriction: Registration is limited to  students registered in the Studio Art Major with  an average of 70% in all ARTH and SART course  attempts. This is a Priority Access Course. SART*4410.Title: SART*4410 Printmaking III (0.5 Credits)
SART*4410.Description: Contemporary issues in printmaking will be addressed through studio projects, readings and independent work in close consultation with the instructor. Interdisciplinary projects will be encouraged using any of the techniques studied in printmaking to this point. Conceptual approaches, including prints and installation, modular and sculptural applications can be explored.
SART*4410.Restriction: Registration is limited to  students registered in the Studio Art Major with  an average of 70% in all ARTH and SART course  attempts. This is a Priority Access Course. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.

SART*4810.Title: SART*4810 Experimental Studio III (0.5 Credits)
SART*4810.Description: This course will consist of thematic projects that elaborate on issues and practices that are timely and significant to contemporary art. In a context of critical reading, writing, class exercise and discussion - students will be encouraged to consider various forms and media to realize their ideas. Students will continue developing their technical skills in video and sound production and are encouraged to explore such forms as collage, assemblage, the artist book and/or multiple, performance, social practice art, interventions, and other "post-studio" and experimental studio strategies.
SART*4810.Restriction: Registration is limited to students registered in the Studio Art Major with an average of 70% in all ARTH and SART course attempts. SART*4900.Title: SART*4900 Critical Practices: Studio Art (1 Credits)
SART*4900.Description: This capstone Studio Art course is an advanced and specialized program that encourages individual studio work, interdisciplinary and collaboration, and the development of independent study strategies. Students undertake a major self-directed project, preparing them for graduate school and professional pursuits in the Arts. While primarily self-directed, weekly classes include seminars, lectures and student presentations with a focus on contemporary art.

SART*4910.Title: SART*4910 Independent Studio (1 Credits)
SART*4910.Description: This capstone course emphasizes individual studio work, interdisciplinary collaboration, and independent study strategies by completing a major self-directed project. The course also includes seminars on professional skills for artists and concludes with a group exhibition organized by participants.
SART*4910.Restriction: Restricted to SART majors with an average of 70% in all ARTH and SART course attempts. This course cannot be taken concurrently with SART*4900. Students are initially restricted to two SART courses per semester. For registration in additional SART classes, contact the SART Faculty Advisor.

SART*4910.Requisites: 2 of SART*4090, SART*4200, SART*4300, SART*4410, SART*4700, SART*4810   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOAN*2111.Title: SOAN*2111 Classical Theory (0.5 Credits)
SOAN*2111.Description: First part of the two-semester course SOAN*2111/2. This course explores the origins and early development of sociological theory in its classical and early contemporary traditions. When you select it you must select SOAN*2111 in the Fall semester and SOAN*2112 in the Winter semester. A grade will not be assigned to SOAN*2111 until SOAN*2112 has been completed.
SOAN*2111.Requisites:
1 of ANTH*1150, SOC*1100, SOC*1500
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOAN*2120.Title: SOAN*2120 Introductory Methods (0.5 Credits)
SOAN*2120.Description: A general introduction to the process of social research emphasizing research design, techniques of data collection, analysis and interpretation of research results.
SOAN*2120.Requisites: 1 of ANTH*1150, CJPP*1000, IDEV*1000, SOC*1000, SOC*1100, SOC*1500   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOAN*2400.Title: SOAN*2400 Introduction to Gender Systems (0.5 Credits)
SOAN*2400.Description: An introduction to the examination of the characteristics of gender relationships both historically and cross-culturally. Amongst the emphases are theoretical approaches to gender analysis, methodologies, case studies and attention to themes such as class and stratification, race and ethnicity, identities and global restructuring as these shape gender dynamics.
SOAN*2400.Offering: Also offered through  Distance Education format.
SOAN*2400.Requisites: 1 of ANTH*1150, IDEV*1000, SOC*1100   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOAN*3040.Title: SOAN*3040 Globalization, Work & Orgs (0.5 Credits)
SOAN*3040.Description: This course examines the social, economic, and political dimensions of work, locating work and its transformation within the broader context of globalization, economic restructuring, and shifts in public policy. Theoretical approaches and concepts used in the study of work will be introduced and critically assessed.
SOAN*3040.Requisites: 1 of ANTH*2160, ANTH*2180, SOAN*2112   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOAN*3100.Title: SOAN*3100 Gender Perspectives/Families (0.5 Credits)
SOAN*3100.Description: This course explores families and households from a gender perspective, using insights from sociology and anthropology.
SOAN*3100.Requisites: (1 of ANTH*2160, ANTH*2180, SOAN*2112, SOAN*2400), (POLS*2650 or SOAN*2120)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOAN*3120.Title: SOAN*3120 Quantitative Methods (0.5 Credits)
SOAN*3120.Description: This course introduces basic descriptive and inferential techniques used in quantitative social research. Students will acquire the skills needed to perform basic analyses and to read the research literature. They will also acquire skills in using a standard computer package to perform data analyses. Topics include: data organization, sample description, hypothesis testing and measures of association.
SOAN*3120.Requisites:
SOAN*2120
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*1000.Title: SOC*1000 Topics in Criminal Justice (0.5 Credits)
SOC*1000.Description: This introductory course will address some of the most pressing issues in criminology and criminal justice today. It will examine the causes and consequences of crime and criminalization.
SOC*1000.Restriction: This is a Priority Access course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or semester levels during certain periods.

SOC*1100.Title: SOC*1100 Sociology (0.5 Credits)
SOC*1100.Description: An introductory course dealing with the basic concepts and methods of sociology applied to societies, groups and individuals. Students will gain an understanding of basic social processes such as socialization, social exchange, deviance and conformity, social change and basic social institutions such as the economy, the polity, the family, religion, education.
SOC*1100.Offering: Also  offered through Distance Education  format.

SOC*2070.Title: SOC*2070 Social Deviance (0.5 Credits)
SOC*2070.Description: An introduction to some of the basic theories of deviance and social control and their application to selected social problems.
SOC*2070.Offering: Also  offered through Distance Education  format.
SOC*2070.Restriction: This is a Priority  Access Course. Enrolment may be restricted to  particular programs or specializations. Please  see the departmental website.
SOC*2070.Requisites:
SOC*1100 or SOC*1500
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*2280.Title: SOC*2280 Society, Knowledge Sys & Env (0.5 Credits)
SOC*2280.Description: This course provides students with an introduction to the nature and dimensions of the environmental crisis by examining knowledge systems and their relationships with the environment. These foundations are intended to enable respective, respectful, reciprocal, and meaningful engagement between Indigenous and science-based knowledge systems in cross-cultural environmental stewardship/governance. Issues to be examined may include climate change and variability, nuclear energy, environmental toxins, species extinction, and population growth pressures.
SOC*2280.Offering: Also offered through Distance Education format.
SOC*2280.Requisites: 1 of ANTH*1150, GEOG*1220, IDEV*1000, INDG*1000, SOC*1100   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*2390.Title: SOC*2390 Class and Stratification (0.5 Credits)
SOC*2390.Description: An examination of the persistent bases of social inequalities such as wealth, income, power and prestige including class formation, class consciousness, political activity and social mobility.
SOC*2390.Requisites:
SOC*1100
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*2700.Title: SOC*2700 Criminological Theory (0.5 Credits)
SOC*2700.Description: This course will examine the development of criminological theory from the late 1700s to contemporary times.
SOC*2700.Requisites: 1 of CJPP*1000, SOC*1000, SOC*1500   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*2760.Title: SOC*2760 Homicide (0.5 Credits)
SOC*2760.Description: This course will review legal definitions of homicide, statistical trends in homicide-both in Canada and internationally-and theoretical explanations of homicide. The course will also examine the key criminological/ sociological empirical research studies on the various types of homicide, such as: femicide, familialcide, serial and mass murder.
SOC*2760.Restriction: This is a Priority Access  Course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular  programs or specializations. Please see the  departmental website for more  information.

SOC*2900.Title: SOC*2900 Current Topics in Sociology (0.5 Credits)
SOC*2900.Description: This course examines recent research and public debate on a key topic in sociology. Students will explore current events through a sociological lens while learning to assess social research and apply concepts. Topics will vary from semester to semester and will be announced before course selection.
SOC*2900.Restriction: This is a Priority Access course. Enrolment may be restricted to particular programs or specializations. Please see the departmental website.
SOC*2900.Requisites: 4.00 credits   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*3310.Title: SOC*3310 Contemporary Theory (0.5 Credits)
SOC*3310.Description: This course outlines and evaluates the major theories in use today. A central aspect of the course is instruction in the application of these theories.
SOC*3310.Requisites:
SOAN*2112, SOAN*2120
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*3710.Title: SOC*3710 Youth Justice (0.5 Credits)
SOC*3710.Description: This course examines concerns about youth crime in Canada and elsewhere. It examines the history of legislation to control youth crime, criminal justice processing and practices, public reactions and concerns about youth crime and theoretical models used to explain youth crime.
SOC*3710.Requisites:
(SOAN*2112 or SOC*2700), SOAN*2120
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*3740.Title: SOC*3740 Corrections and Penology (0.5 Credits)
SOC*3740.Description: This course will examine the current state of knowledge regarding the role of corrections and penology. It will examine such specific issues as public perception and reaction to the criminal justice system's methods of punishment and treatment of criminal offenders, the effectiveness of sentencing options and policies, including fines, probation, prison sentences and parole. It will also examine the various theoretical and methodological approaches to the study of courts, corrections and penology.
SOC*3740.Requisites:
(SOAN*2112 or SOC*2700), SOAN*2120
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*3750.Title: SOC*3750 Police in Society (0.5 Credits)
SOC*3750.Description: This course will examine the role of police in society. It will examine theories of policing, the history of policing and such issues as police citizen interaction, relations with visible minorities, methods for controlling police behaviour, and the effectiveness of the police in carrying out specific policy directives.
SOC*3750.Requisites:
(SOAN*2112 or SOC*2700), SOAN*2120
   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*4010.Title: SOC*4010 Violence and Society (0.5 Credits)
SOC*4010.Description: This course will focus on the changing nature of violence in our society by critically evaluating theory, research and public policy on the causes and control of violence. The links among structural, institutional and interpersonal violence will be examined as well as the social construction of violence, particularly why some forms of violence are considered to be more serious social problems than others.

SOC*4130.Description: This advanced seminar offers an in-depth study of the nature of violence in our society.
SOC*4130.Restriction: Restricted to students in BAH.CJPP, BAH.CJPP:C and BAH.SOC with an average of 70% in all course attempts in Sociology and Sociology and Anthropology courses. SOC*4150.Title: SOC*4150 Youth and Violence (1 Credits)
SOC*4150.Description: This course is a sociological exploration of youth violence, considering current explanations of youth violence, the sociological implications of Canada's juvenile justice system and policies impacting youth, and the influence of media, family and school. Reform initiatives and justice alternatives aimed at youth will also be examined.
SOC*4150.Restriction: Restricted to students in BAH.CJPP, BAH.CJPP:C and BAH.SOC with an average of 70% in all course attempts in Sociology and Sociology and Anthropology courses. SOC*4150.Requisites: 14.00 credits including (POLS*3650 or SOAN*3120), (SOC*2700 or SOC*3310)   - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

SOC*4320.Title: SOC*4320 Adv Sem in Criminal Justice (1 Credits)
SOC*4320.Description: This advanced seminar offers an in-depth study of issues in criminal justice.
SOC*4320.Restriction: Restricted to students in BAH.CJPP and BAH.CJPP:C. CJPP and CJPP:C students are restricted to a maximum of 3.00 credits in SOC and POLS 4000-level CJPP restricted electives.
